frameworks.name: Four Acquisition Targets Framework
frameworks.definition: Acquisition.com targets four categories of high-cash-flow service businesses: e-learning businesses in niches, brick-and-mortar chains with multiple existing locations, tech-enabled services (SaaS or software-adjacent), and consumer experience businesses.

frameworks.name: Photographer Studio Expansion Model
frameworks.definition: A capital-deployment model where the parent company funds the opening of new studio locations while the founder focuses on replication of a proven experiential service delivery model, converting B2B coaching revenue into high-margin B2C location expansion.

claims.text: Alex Hormozi prioritizes high-cash-flow service businesses over software because service businesses allow rapid changes to pricing, product, and client experience without engineering work, maintaining simple unit economics with easily-captured high margins.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
claims.mechanism: Service businesses are inherently more malleable than software, allowing margin capture without technical leverage
bounded_by: Does not apply to software/SaaS businesses where pricing and product changes require engineering effort
Does not apply to businesses requiring significant R&D or UX work

claims.text: Acquisition.com deploys a minority-stake acquisition model: taking 20% ownership in businesses already operating at scale in their category (legal, hair salons, photography), then applying a proven scaling playbook to move them from single-location to multi-location operations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Target business must already be proven and operating profitably
claims.mechanism: The founder of the acquired business has already validated the unit economics and service delivery; Hormozi brings scaling systems without needing to build the business from zero

claims.text: Photo studio chains represent the highest-potential acquisition target because they combine high unit economics (studio margins exceed $100k+), low capital requirements ($X cost to open vs. $Y revenue per location), mission-driven founder psychology (which sustains effort through scaling), and the ability to rapidly open new locations.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Requires proven unit economics at single location
claims.mechanism: Mission-driven founders have intrinsic motivation to scale rather than extract value, enabling rapid multi-location rollout with minimal founder fatigue

anchors.value: 1 location at acquisition; 13 locations approximately 1 year later

claims.text: When evaluating acquisition targets, Hormozi rejected B2B coaching-based business models ($5k per customer) in favor of B2C photo studio models because photographer studios generate significantly higher revenue per customer through productized storybook experience packages sold at point of sale.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Comparing B2B coaching revenue model to B2C retail photography
claims.mechanism: B2C point-of-sale transactions generate higher customer lifetime value and repeat purchase than B2B consulting-based engagement

anchors.value: Substantially higher per-customer lifetime revenue (exact figures withheld)

bounded_by: Specific comparison is between these two business models; does not generalize to all B2B vs B2C

claims.text: Brick-and-mortar chains with multiple already-successful locations represent an acquisition sweet spot because they have de-risked unit economics and require capital deployment rather than business model validation.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business must have 2+ successful existing locations
claims.mechanism: Multi-location validation removes demand-risk and execution-risk, leaving only capital availability and scaling discipline as variables

claims.text: Photographer studio expansion is structured as full acquisition (100% ownership) rather than minority stake because capital requirements to open new locations are lower than studio profit margin, enabling rapid location multiplication while the parent company retains complete control.
claims.speaker: Alex Hormozi
conditions: Business model has low capital-per-location cost relative to per-location profit
claims.mechanism: When capital cost < per-location profit, the parent company can fund all expansion from a single location's cash flow without diluting ownership
bounded_by: Only applicable when capital cost per location is substantially below profit per location

examples.text: The Magic Chains photography business was founded by mission-driven entrepreneurs whose daughter stopped speaking after being told she was stupid at school. The founders began photographing her and creating storybook experiences where she was the hero; their daughter regained her speech by reading her own story. This inspired them to commercialize the concept as a consumer service (the Magic Chains storybook photo experience), which Hormozi then funded from one location to thirteen locations in approximately one year after acquiring a 20% stake—demonstrating rapid scaling with the mission-driven founder psychology retained throughout expansion.

At the time of acquisition, the photography business founder was running a separate B2B side business (selling coaching and business consulting for approximately $5k per customer). Hormozi identified that photographer studio margins were substantially higher and rejected continuing the B2B coaching model entirely, instead doubling down on opening new B2C photo studio locations. This shift consolidated the founder's focus and aligned revenue model with the acquisition thesis.

practices.text: When evaluating acquisition targets, calculate the cost to open a new location and compare it to the profit per location. If cost << profit, the business is acquisition-eligible for rapid multi-location expansion funded by the parent company.

Target acquisition opportunities in service categories where the founder has already proven multi-location scalability (brick-and-mortar chains with 2+ existing locations), rather than single-location businesses requiring model validation.
